autocorrelation.simple: How strongly a series is related to its own past values.
autocorrelation.example: If today's temperature is close to yesterday's, the series has high autocorrelation.

cross-sectional.simple: Data about many things at one moment in time.
cross-sectional.example: The height of 1,000 people measured today.

panel data.simple: Data about many things, each measured at many moments. It is many time series in one table.

frequency.simple: The size of the time step of a series.

irregular time series.simple: A series whose time steps are not equal, such as a log of events.
irregular time series.example: The exact times when customers buy something.

trend.simple: The long-run direction of a series: going up, going down, or flat.
trend.example: The number of app users grows every year.

seasonality.simple: A pattern that repeats with a fixed, known period.
seasonality.example: Sales are high every Saturday (period 7 days).

cycle.simple: Rises and falls that repeat but with no fixed length.

noise.simple: The random part of a series that no model can predict.
noise.example: Small day-to-day changes caused by luck.

least squares.simple: A way to fit a line: choose the line that makes the sum of squared gaps to the data as small as possible.

additive model.simple: A model where the parts are added: y = trend + season + noise.
additive model.example: Swings of the season keep the same size at all levels.

multiplicative model.simple: A model where the parts are multiplied: y = trend × season × noise.
multiplicative model.example: Summer sales are 20% above normal, so swings grow with the level.

downsampling.simple: Reducing the number of points of a series, for example hourly to daily by combining rows, or to draw a chart.
downsampling.example: s.resample('D').sum() turns hourly rows into daily rows.

upsampling.simple: Changing a series to a finer time step. New rows have no data until you fill them.
upsampling.example: Monthly data turned into daily data with ffill.

linear interpolation.simple: Filling a gap with a straight line between the known value before it and the known value after it.
linear interpolation.example: 10 on day 0 and 16 on day 3 gives 12 on day 1 and 14 on day 2.

data leakage.simple: Using information in a feature or in training that you would not have at prediction time. Scores look good but fail in real use.
data leakage.example: A rolling mean that includes today's value, when you predict today.

lag.simple: A value from k steps in the past. Lag 1 is the previous value.

difference.simple: The change from one step to the next: y(t) − y(t−1). It removes a trend.

return.simple: The relative change of a price: p(t) / p(t−1) − 1.
return.example: Price 100 to 110 is a return of 0.10 (10%).

log return.simple: The natural log of the price ratio: ln(p(t) / p(t−1)). Log returns add up over time.

rolling window.simple: A window of the last k rows that moves forward one row at a time. You compute one number per window.

EWMA.simple: Exponentially weighted moving average: a smoothed value where new data get weight alpha and older data fade out.
EWMA.example: s = 0.3 * x + 0.7 * s, or s.ewm(alpha=0.3, adjust=False).mean()

decomposition.simple: Splitting a series into trend, seasonal part and remainder.
decomposition.example: Monthly sales = growth + yearly wave + random rest.

STL.simple: Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess. It splits a series into trend, season and residual parts, and the season can change slowly.

loess.simple: A smoothing method that fits many small local lines to nearby points.
loess.example: STL uses loess to estimate the trend and the season.
